draft.title: The natural rate of unemployment
card: The natural rate of unemployment is the rate below which unemployment cannot fall without inflation rising. It is not zero, because some unemployment exists in any working economy.
Frictional
people between jobs or new to the workforce, who are looking for a good match. It lasts a short time.
Seasonal
job loss from regular changes in demand through the year, such as fruit pickers after harvest.
Structural
a mismatch between workers' skills or location and the jobs available, often after an industry shrinks. Together these three make up the natural rate, and estimates for Australia change over time.
draft.remember: The natural rate is not zero: it is the lowest unemployment that can last without pushing inflation up.

a.q: What does the natural rate of unemployment measure?
opts: The lowest rate that can last without inflation rising
The rate at which every person who wants a job has one
The rate at which inflation in the economy falls to zero
The average rate recorded over the past ten years
a.why: The natural rate is the floor that unemployment cannot fall below without inflation rising. It is not zero, so it does not mean everyone has a job. It is also not a past average, because estimates for it change over time.
a.clue: Think about what happens to inflation if unemployment falls too low.

b.q: A car plant in Geelong closes. Its workers have skills the local job market no longer needs. Which type of unemployment is this?
opts: Structural unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
Hidden unemployment
b.why: The workers' skills do not match the jobs available after an industry shrinks, which is structural unemployment. Frictional is the most tempting wrong answer, but it describes short searches by people who have suitable jobs open to them.
b.clue: Ask whether the problem is a short search or a lasting mismatch of skills.

a.best: The lowest rate that can last without inflation rising

problems.detail: Why (a) argues the natural rate is not a past average 'because estimates for it change over time'. That does not follow, since a ten-year average also changes over time. The real reason is that it is defined by its link to inflation, not by past data.
